content: The following are professional interpretations of the provided references: 1. A study in Bangladesh explored the factors influencing the recruitment and retention of community health workers involved in a newborn care intervention. This research was published in Human Resources for Health and accessed on January 24, 2021. 2. Abbey and colleagues investigated the retention of community health workers in a trial focused on community-based fever management in children under five years in Ghana's Dangme West district. The findings were published in International Health and accessed on January 24, 2021. 3. Watanabe and co-authors examined the impact of information technology on the physician workforce and healthcare delivery in isolated Canadian communities. This study was published in the Journal of Telemedicine and Telecare and accessed on January 25, 2021. 4. Gruen and colleagues reviewed the role of specialist outreach clinics in primary care and rural hospital settings. Their systematic review was published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews in 2003 and accessed on January 25, 2021. 5. Gagnon and co-authors conducted a qualitative case study to explore the effects of telehealth on the supply of medical human resources in remote regions. This research was published in BMC Health Services Research in 2007. 6. Another study by Gagnon and colleagues identified the conditions necessary for successfully implementing telehealth to support medical practice in rural and remote areas. This work was published in Implementation Science and accessed on January 25, 2021. 7. Mbemba and co-authors conducted a longitudinal study in Mali to assess the influence of a telehealth project on healthcare professional recruitment and retention in remote areas. The findings were published in SAGE Open Medicine in 2016. 8. Komaromy and colleagues introduced Project ECHO, a model designed to educate primary care providers on treating substance use disorders. This study was published in Substance Abuse and accessed on January 25, 2021. 9. Bagayoko and co-authors shared lessons from the EQUi-ResHuS project in Mali, which used e-health as a mechanism to recruit and retain healthcare professionals in remote areas. This research was published in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making. 10. Bervell and Al-Samarraie conducted a comparative review of mobile health and electronic health utilization in sub-Saharan African countries. Their findings were published in Social Science and Medicine in 2019. 11. Ly and colleagues explored the individual and contextual factors influencing the use of telemedicine in Senegal. Their descriptive study focused on the perceptions of physicians and telemedicine project managers and was published in PLOS One in 2017. 12. The Global Observatory for eHealth published a report titled mHealth: New Horizons for Health Through Mobile Technologies, which was accessed on January 25, 2021. 13. Masango and colleagues assessed the role of non-financial incentives in retaining Swaziland's health sector workforce. Their findings were published in the EQUINET Discussion Paper series. 14. Butterworth and co-authors conducted a qualitative study on the retention of general practitioners in rural Nepal. This research was published in the Australian Journal of Rural Health in 2008. 15. Connolly and colleagues examined the impact of longitudinal rural medical student clerkships on clinical supervisors and hospitals. Their findings were published in the Australian Journal of Rural Health in 2014. 16. Levesque and co-authors explored physician perceptions of recruitment and retention factors in areas with regional medical campuses. This study was published in the Canadian Medical Education Journal in 2018. 17. Couper and Worley discussed the role of the journal Rural and Remote Health in addressing health and information challenges in Africa. Their work was published in 2006. 18. Wibulpolprasert and Pengpaibon reviewed four decades of integrated strategies to address the inequitable distribution of doctors in Thailand. Their findings were published in Human Resources for Health. 19. Gardiner and colleagues evaluated the impact of support initiatives on retaining rural general practitioners. This study was published in the Australian Journal of Rural Health in 2006. 20. Willis-Shattuck and co-authors conducted a systematic review on the motivation and retention of health workers in developing countries. Their findings were published in BMC Health Services Research. 21. The World Health Organization, World Bank, and USAID published a user guide on conducting discrete choice experiments for health workforce recruitment and retention in remote and rural areas. This guide includes case studies and was accessed on January 25, 2021. 22. Robyn and colleagues used a discrete choice experiment to develop rural retention strategies for health workers in Cameroon. Their findings were published in the International Journal of Health Policy and Management. 23. Abdel-All and co-authors conducted a discrete choice experiment to understand the preferences of community health workers, specifically accredited social health activists (ASHAs) in India. This study was published in BMJ Global Health. 24. Mandeville and colleagues systematically reviewed the use of discrete choice experiments to inform health workforce policy. Their findings were published in BMC Health Services Research in 2014. 25. Bowen and co-authors outlined methods for designing feasibility studies in healthcare research. Their work was published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine. 26. Dal Poz and colleagues edited a handbook on monitoring and evaluating human resources for health, with a focus on lowand middle-income countries. This resource was accessed on January 25, 2021. 27. Buchan reviewed the benefits of health workforce stability in a study published in Human Resources for Health in 2010. 28. Lewin and co-authors introduced the GRADE-CERQual approach for applying qualitative evidence synthesis findings. Their work was published in Implementation Science.
